extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers interested in manners, wit, and social satire (general public of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and principles for producing or judging social wit, raillery, public entertainments, and the moral use of talents in the manner of The Spectator essays. Emphasises target selection, propriety, and the moral ends of skillful expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of talents depends on their application
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Gifts of Nature and Accomplishments of Art are valuable, but as they are exerted in the Interest of Virtue, or governed by the Rules of Honour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talents and accomplishments should be judged by how they are used. Skill employed for virtuous or honourable ends merits admiration; the same skill used to promote vice, deceit, or triviality loses its honour. Examples given: artistic execution should serve noble subjects rather than preserve lewd devices or monsters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be carried away by mere beauty or wit
rubrics_metrics.description: “We ought to abstract our Minds from the Observation of any Excellence ... till we have taken some Notice ... of the Disposition of their Minds; otherwise the Beauty of their Persons, or the Charms of their Wit, may make us fond of those whom our Reason and Judgment will tell us we ought to abhor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before admiring someone for physical beauty or cleverness, assess their moral disposition and intentions. Superficial attractions should not override reasoned judgment; otherwise one risks valuing people one ought to condemn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity or immodesty diminishes admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: “The wanton Carriage in a Woman, would disappoint her of the Admiration which she aims at; and the vain Dress or Discourse of a Man would destroy the Comeliness of his Shape, or Goodness of his Understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty and restraint preserve the positive effects of beauty and sense. Display, affectation, or immodesty undermine the very qualities that draw admiration and therefore reduce one's social esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention should be the primary measure of approbation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Were the Intention stedfastly considered, as the Measure of Approbation, all Falsehood would soon be out of Countenance; and an Address in imposing upon Mankind, would be as contemptible in one State of Life as another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge actions by the actor's intent: honest, dutiful intentions deserve approbation even if results vary; artifice and deceit should be equally censured across ranks. This principle is recommended as a corrective to praising mere effectiveness without moral regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: True glory relies on patience, conscience, and independence from applause
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is but one thing necessary to keep the Possession of true Glory, which is, to hear the Opposers of it with Patience, and preserve the Virtue by which it was acquired... He only is a great Man who can neglect the Applause of the Multitude, and enjoy himself independent of its Favour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enduring reputation rests on preserving virtue and composure under criticism rather than seeking popular applause. Practitioners of wit or public acts should aim for inward approval of duty rather than external triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not promote silly or immoral competitions; prize useful accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning whether proposing prizes for 'useless Accomplishments' (e.g., grinning matches, running asses, grinning-for-a-ring) is an affront to the species and 'has not in it something Immoral as well as Ridiculous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public entertainments and contests should aim to improve useful skills or public good (e.g., handicraft prizes for manufactures) rather than rewarding deformity, vulgarity, or vanity. Organisers should consider moral and social effects before creating prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce fairness: disqualify cheats in competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by the ploughman who 'practised with Verjuice' and had a 'Crab found upon him at the very time of Grinning,' who was declared a cheat and set aside by judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions require scrutiny and fair judging; evident artifices or preparations that give an unfair advantage should be treated as cheating and lead to disqualification to preserve the integrity of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: When engaging in raillery, assess both your target and yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best Rule I can lay down for them to avoid the like Calamities for the future, is thoroughly to consider not only Whether their Companions are weak, but Whether themselves are Wits.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting witty raillery or mockery, ensure the person targeted is a suitable (weak/vulnerable) butt and that you possess sufficient wit to avoid being bested. Failure to self-assess risks humiliation and social harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose targets and timing carefully (mark the 'butts')
rubrics_metrics.description: The (humorous) proposal that 'all Butts should wear an Inscription affixed ... shewing on which Side they are to be come at,' so people would know when it is safe to attack them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tongue-in-cheek recommendation emphasizes the pragmatic point: satire and mockery should be directed at appropriate personalities and moments. Consider temperament and context; avoid attacking when it is socially or morally inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value should be gauged by numbers and reasoned calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Numbers are so much the Measure of every thing that is valuable, that it is not possible to demonstrate the Success of any Action, or the Prudence of any Undertaking, without them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In matters of commerce, patronage, or organising public projects (including prizes or entertainments with economic effects), use quantitative reasoning (accounts, estimates of demand, costs, returns) to judge prudence and value rather than mere appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to detraction patiently preserves merit
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where an eminent Merit is robbed by Artifice or Detraction, it does but encrease by such Endeavours of its Enemies... The impotent Pains which are taken to sully it... will naturally produce the contrary Effect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When merit is attacked by false artifice or slander, maintain patience and preserve the virtue by which it was acquired; efforts to sully true merit often backfire and increase its luster. This is recommended as a strategic and moral response to criticism.
